name: Wireless & Cellular Security
description: Security of cellular (4G/5G), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and other RF/wireless protocols.
narrative:
The earliest papers in this list mark wireless security's pivot from informal probing to rigorous, systematic scrutiny of cellular standards. On the formal side, "A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication" (CCS 2018) used symbolic model checking to expose weaknesses in the 5G AKA protocol even before deployment, while "LTEInspector" (NDSS 2018) paired a model checker with a real testbed to uncover practical attacks on 4G attach, detach, and paging. In parallel, hands-on work showed these protocols were exploitable in the field: "Breaking LTE on Layer Two" (S&P 2019) revealed that LTE's unauthenticated layer-two could be manipulated to redirect and fingerprint traffic, and "Hiding in Plain Signal" (USENIX 2019) demonstrated overshadowing a legitimate LTE signal over the air. Beyond cellular, this period also surfaced the broader RF attack surface: "All Your GPS Are Belong To Us" (USENIX 2018) showed stealthy road-navigation spoofing, and "Screaming Channels" (CCS 2018) found that electromagnetic side channels can leak secrets straight through the radios of Bluetooth and Wi-Fi chips.

A clear shift followed: formal analysis and dynamic testing became the dominant methodology, fanning out across venues. "5GReasoner" (CCS 2019) and "Component-Based Formal Analysis of 5G-AKA" (NDSS 2019) extended property-directed verification deeper into the 5G stack, while "Touching the Untouchables" (S&P 2019) built dynamic testing of the LTE control plane. Privacy emerged as its own thread, with "GUTI Reallocation Demystified" (NDSS 2018) and "Privacy Attacks to the 4G and 5G Cellular Paging Protocols" (NDSS 2019) turning temporary identifiers and paging side channels into location-tracking attacks. The short-range wireless world saw the same maturation: "The KNOB is Broken" (USENIX 2019) and "BIAS" (S&P 2020) broke Bluetooth's key negotiation and impersonation guarantees, "Dragonblood" (S&P 2020) cracked the WPA3 handshake, and "Frankenstein" (USENIX 2020) brought advanced fuzzing to Bluetooth firmware.

By the early 2020s the field broadened in two directions: down into implementations and out to new physical domains. Instead of only analyzing standards, researchers attacked real silicon and firmware — "FirmXRay" (CCS 2020) mined BLE bugs from bare-metal firmware, "FirmWire" (NDSS 2022) made cellular baseband firmware transparently analyzable, and "Noncompliance as Deviant Behavior" (CCS 2021) automatically caught devices that deviate from the LTE spec. Attacks also moved past traditional protocols to satellites and sensing: "A Tale of Sea and Sky" (S&P 2020) and "Space Odyssey" (S&P 2023) opened up maritime VSAT and satellite security, while "mmSpy" (S&P 2022) and "IRShield" (S&P 2022) showed how mmWave and physical-layer sensing can both attack and defend privacy. Practical eavesdropping landed too, with "Call Me Maybe" (USENIX 2020) decrypting real VoLTE calls via key reuse.

Where the area stands now is a balance between offense, deployment-grade realism, and defense. GPS work matured from lab spoofing to real-world demonstrations, as in "An Experimental Study of GPS Spoofing and Takeover Attacks on UAVs" (USENIX 2022), and 5G research began proposing fixes rather than only breaks, e.g. "Privacy-Preserving and Standard-Compatible AKA Protocol for 5G" (USENIX 2021). The frontier has also absorbed machine learning, with "Robust Adversarial Attacks Against DNN-Based Wireless Communication Systems" (CCS 2021), and countermeasures like "IRShield" signal a growing emphasis on protecting users against the very physical-layer leakage earlier work exposed. Across a decade and four top venues, the arc runs from formally breaking standards, to exploiting them over the air, to digging into firmware and silicon, to securing an ever-widening set of RF systems from cellular to satellites.

milestones.title: LTEInspector: A Systematic Approach for Adversarial Testing of 4G LTE
milestones.note: pioneered combining model checking with a real testbed to systematically find practical 4G LTE attacks

milestones.title: A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication
milestones.note: brought rigorous symbolic verification to the 5G AKA standard before deployment, setting the formal-analysis agenda

milestones.title: Breaking LTE on Layer Two
milestones.note: showed LTE's unauthenticated layer-two enables real over-the-air redirection and traffic fingerprinting

milestones.title: The KNOB is Broken: Exploiting Low Entropy in the Encryption Key Negotiation Of Bluetooth BR/EDR
milestones.note: exposed a standard-level flaw letting attackers force low-entropy Bluetooth keys across billions of devices

milestones.title: Dragonblood: Analyzing the Dragonfly Handshake of WPA3 and EAP-pwd
milestones.note: broke the newly standardized WPA3 handshake, showing next-gen Wi-Fi security shipped with exploitable flaws

milestones.title: Call Me Maybe: Eavesdropping Encrypted LTE Calls With ReVoLTE
milestones.note: demonstrated decrypting real encrypted VoLTE calls via keystream reuse, a deployed-network eavesdropping attack

milestones.title: FirmWire: Transparent Dynamic Analysis for Cellular Baseband Firmware
milestones.note: shifted analysis from standards to silicon by making baseband firmware transparently fuzzable

milestones.title: An Experimental Study of GPS Spoofing and Takeover Attacks on UAVs
milestones.note: moved GPS spoofing from lab feasibility to real-world UAV takeover, grounding RF attacks in deployment realism
